About

Hongjia Liu

Physiological sensing · Machine learning · AI for health

I am an undergraduate in Intelligent Medical Engineering at Southern University of Science and Technology (SUSTech), and I am currently an exchange student at UC San Diego for Fall 2026. At SUSTech’s Contactless Healthcare Lab, I work with Prof. Wenjin Wang on camera-based physiological sensing and biomedical signal analysis.

My interests lie at the intersection of physiological sensing and AI: learning useful representations from physiological data and understanding how measurement conditions affect what models can learn. My experience spans optical sensing experiments, EEG emotion recognition, ECG classification, and robotic camera systems. I am seeking PhD opportunities for Fall 2027.

Research

Experimental systems, signal analysis, and physiological interpretation.

Jul 2025 – Present · First author · Submitted to IEEE TBioCAS

Effects of Illumination Geometry on Multi-Wavelength PPG Imaging

How does the way we illuminate tissue change the physiological information captured by a camera?

Approach. I developed a dual-mode, multi-wavelength finger-imaging system and a signal-processing framework to compare contact and non-contact illumination. The study involved 37 participants and examined amplitude-based oxygenation measurements and phase-based multi-wavelength pulse transit time (MW-PTT).

My contribution. I built the acquisition and analysis framework and compared wavelength-unified and wavelength-specific regions of interest. The experiments combined breath-holding and cold-pressor protocols with AC/DC feature extraction, ratio-of-ratios calibration, and pulse timing analysis.

Findings. Contact illumination favored AC-based SpO₂ estimation, while non-contact illumination favored DC-based models and produced larger, more stable MW-PTT responses. The work highlights the importance of preserving comparable optical sampling across wavelengths rather than selecting each wavelength solely for its strongest signal.

Mar 2025 – Jan 2026 · First author · EMBC 2026 accepted

Spatial Analysis of rPPG Under Contact and Non-Contact Illumination

Where do useful physiological signals form, and how does their location change across wavelengths?

Approach. I developed a dual-mode rPPG imaging setup and a spatial heatmap analysis framework, evaluated in 15 participants. Pixel-level maps of AC, DC, AC/DC, and MW-PTT were paired with statistical analysis along the normalized distance from the light source.

My contribution. I implemented the spatial analysis pipeline to compare signal amplitude, normalized pulsatility, and inter-wavelength timing under the two lighting conditions. This connected regional signal patterns to the optical configuration rather than relying on a single averaged waveform.

Findings. Non-contact illumination produced comparatively uniform spatial patterns. Contact illumination produced strong distance- and wavelength-dependent patterns, including rise-and-fall profiles in AC/DC and MW-PTT. These results motivate careful region selection and wavelength-aware interpretation of rPPG measurements.

Sep 2024 – Feb 2025 · Third author · EMBC 2025

SpO₂ Monitoring via Time-Division Multiplexed Near-Infrared Imaging

Can the slowly varying component of camera signals help track changes in blood oxygen saturation?

Approach. The system used one camera with sequential 750, 800, and 940 nm illumination to compare pulsatile (AC) and non-pulsatile (DC) oxygenation features. Eleven participants completed a breath-holding protocol, and calibration was evaluated with leave-one-subject-out testing.

My contribution. I contributed to multi-wavelength signal analysis and SpO₂ calibration, including investigation of temperature-induced camera baseline drift. This project developed my experience in experimental sensing, calibration, and interpreting sources of measurement error.

Findings. In this study, the 750/940 nm DC-based model achieved a mean absolute error of 1.63%, compared with 2.55% for the AC-based model. The results support the feasibility of DC-based calibration in the tested setup; they do not establish general performance across devices or clinical populations.

Selected Projects

Course projects in machine learning, signal processing, and robotics.

Machine Learning and its Medical Engineering Applications · Course project

EEG Emotion Recognition with ST-SHAP

I adapted the Swin Transformer-based ST-SHAP framework to the EmoEEG-MC dataset for three- and seven-class emotion recognition. The pipeline converts differential entropy features into 32 × 32 scalp maps and stacks four consecutive temporal frames as input channels to a hierarchical Swin model.

64-channel EEG→DE scalp maps × 4 frames→Swin Transformer→Emotion classes + SHAP

I compared five frequency bands across video, imagery, and combined settings, and used SHAP to examine which time segments contributed to predictions. The fourth segment contributed most in the analyzed attribution results.

Evaluation. Selected three-class experiments reached peak within-subject accuracy above 95% and leave-one-subject-out accuracy above 50%. These are peak results from selected runs, not full-cohort averages. The comparison emphasizes the challenge of generalizing across people.

Medical Robotics · Course project

Active-Vision Camera Robot for Physiological Monitoring

I contributed to the design of a camera robot that aims to maintain a frontal view of the face during treadmill exercise. The design combines a two-degree-of-freedom positioning platform with a three-degree-of-freedom stereo-camera module to compensate for changes in head position, orientation, and viewing distance.

My contribution. I developed SolidWorks models of the robotic assembly, established a Denavit–Hartenberg forward kinematic model, and used MATLAB to simulate reachable workspace and camera motion.

Outcome. The project connects sensing requirements to mechanical design and kinematic analysis. It is a design and simulation project; improved physiological measurement accuracy during exercise has not been experimentally established.

Digital Signal Processing · Course project

ECG Signal Processing and Arrhythmia Classification

I implemented a MATLAB pipeline for MIT-BIH ECG analysis: IIR/FIR filtering, R-peak detection, QRS and RR feature extraction, heart rate variability analysis, and SVM classification. Comparing the filter designs highlighted the trade-off between noise suppression, computational cost, and waveform preservation.

96.36%Five classes · Mixed patient split
79.80%Three classes · Patient-disjoint split

Evaluation. The patient-disjoint experiment tested unseen patients, exposing limitations in cross-patient generalization, particularly for atrial premature beats. Because the two experiments use different class sets as well as different splits, the accuracy values are not a controlled comparison of split strategy alone.
